strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formalized diagnostic framework: the three metrics (reward noise ρnoise, policy-reward coupling ρselfbias, and symmetry bias ρsymbias) provide a principled decomposition of why self-rewarding RL (RLIR) underperforms RLVR, moving beyond anecdotal observations of instability to quantifiable causes.

The controlled decoupling experiments (Sec. 3.5, Fig. 2) that independently vary each metric via synthetic reward injection are a strong methodological choice, isolating causal contributions that would be confounded in standard training runs.

A theoretical result (Appendix C) rigorously characterizes when soft (Freq) vs hard (SC) rewards yield lower MSE relative to the oracle, adding formal grounding to the empirical findings about correctness-confidence effects.

Extensive and fairly thorough empirical validation: multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B), multiple datasets (decontaminated synthetic arithmetic, DAPO-MATH-17K, BigMath, WebInstruct-verified/MMLU-Pro), and numerous ablations (component removal, temperature robustness, interpolation bound sensitivity, ensemble-size scaling, compute/memory analysis).

A decontaminated synthetic arithmetic benchmark and a random-reward control experiment (Fig. 8) help rule out data contamination/memorization as confounds, strengthening the credibility of the reported gains.
Practical deployment consideration: merging the ensemble via TIES-Merging into a single model removes inference-time overhead, making the method more adoptable despite training-time ensemble cost.

Fine-grained ablations (Fig. 5, Table 2, Table 10) convincingly attribute gains to each of the three proposed mechanisms (ensemble rewarding, adaptive interpolation, disagreement-aware selection) rather than treating RLER as a monolithic black box.
weaknesses: The headline aggregate improvement (+6.2% over best RLIR baseline) masks inconsistent per-benchmark performance in Table 1: Co-rewarding beats RLER on AIME25 (11.7 vs 12.1, actually close) and HMMT24 (11.3 vs 9.6), and ties on AIME24 (23.3 vs 23.3), suggesting the advantage is not uniform across tasks and may be sensitive to benchmark composition.

The metrics used both for diagnosis and for validating RLER's improvements (ρnoise, ρselfbias, ρsymbias) require oracle labels r⋆_i to compute, which is in tension with the paper's core motivation of unlabeled/label-scarce settings — these diagnostics are only usable as an offline analysis tool with labeled validation data, not as a deployable training-time signal, and this limitation is not explicitly discussed.

RLER's ensemble design incurs substantial memory overhead that scales roughly linearly with ensemble size k (∼2×–8× VRAM in Table 13), which is a real practical cost for the target scenario of resource-constrained, large-scale unlabeled RL; the paper's compute proxy (Eq. 15) focuses on FLOPs but underplays this memory cost as a primary bottleneck.

The core decoupling experiments demonstrating the causal role of each bias metric (Fig. 2) rely on synthetically injected noise/coupling/skew on a synthetic arithmetic task, rather than directly manipulating naturally arising bias in a real RLIR pipeline; while Fig. 3 shows correlational consistency with real RLIR methods, the causal claims rest primarily on the synthetic injection setting, which may not fully capture the structure of naturally occurring self-rewarding bias.

The method introduces considerable machinery (ensemble aggregation, token-level confidence calibration with batch-wise min-max normalization, adaptive interpolation gate, disagreement-aware rollout allocation/selection, and post-hoc TIES merging), and while ablations show each piece helps, the overall system complexity may hinder reproducibility and adoption relative to simpler baselines.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not engage with any specific ethical or societal considerations relevant to scaling RL on unlabeled/private corpora, which the introduction explicitly motivates as a target use case (e.g., private corpora, industrial applications) and could raise data-governance considerations worth a sentence of discussion.

No wall-clock training time comparisons are reported; the compute analysis relies solely on a FLOPs-based proxy (Eq. 15) and relative memory multipliers, which may not reflect actual training throughput/latency differences between single-policy RLIR and multi-policy RLER in practice.

strengths: Introduces a clear, interpretable diagnostic framework (ρnoise, ρselfbias, ρsymbias) that decomposes RLIR failure modes into noise magnitude, policy-reward coupling, and over-/under-reward skew, providing a principled lens rather than just an empirical fix.

Backs the diagnosis with controlled decoupling experiments (Section 3.5, Fig. 2-3) that isolate each factor causally before proposing a remedy, and further corroborates the 'over-reward is worse than under-reward' claim with a direct oracle-correction study (Appendix B.4, Fig. 9).
Provides theoretical grounding for the soft-vs-hard reward comparison (Section 3.3, Appendix C proof) that explains when Frequency-based rewards outperform Self-Consistency.

RLER is well-motivated by the three desiderata (accuracy, unbiasedness, robustness) and each of its three mechanisms (ensemble rewarding, adaptive interpolation, disagreement-aware selection) is ablated individually (Fig. 5, Table 2, Table 5), showing cumulative contribution.

Broad empirical validation across multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and datasets (synthetic decontaminated arithmetic, DAPO-MATH-17K, BigMath, WebInstruct-verified/MMLU-Pro), plus a random-reward sanity check to rule out contamination/memorization as an explanation of gains.

Practical design choice of merging the ensemble into a single deployable policy (Ties-Merging) removes extra inference cost, and the paper explicitly analyzes compute/memory trade-offs and ensemble-size scaling (Appendix B.3), giving actionable guidance (k=2 default).
weaknesses: Main-table gains (Table 1) are not uniformly dominant per-benchmark (e.g., RLER underperforms Co-rewarding on HMMT24 and ties/loses on some AIME splits); the reported +6.2% is an aggregate Avg@8 improvement, and per-benchmark variance/significance (seeds, error bars) is not reported for Table 1, making the strength of the central comparison harder to assess.

The Judge baseline collapses far below the pretrained model (13.4 vs 25.7 Avg@8), which is surprisingly weak and raises questions about whether all RLIR baselines were tuned comparably, potentially inflating RLER's relative margin.

The synthetic decoupling study (Section 3.5) injects noise via an artificial three-stage process rather than directly deriving from organic RLIR training dynamics; while Fig. 3/4 partially corroborate the findings on real training, the causal isolation still rests on a stylized proxy setting.

Measured ensemble diversity gain (∆div, Table 11) is quite small (~0.02–0.05) despite starting from identical initializations, suggesting the diversity driving the ensemble's benefits may be limited; it is not entirely clear how robust the ensemble mechanism is when diversity is this modest, or whether gains mainly stem from effective doubling of the rollout/estimation pool rather than genuine model diversity.

The approach assumes a well-defined labeling/extraction map ℓ(y) for scoring semantic equivalence across rollouts (verifiable math-style answers or an external verifier); this constrains applicability to open-ended, non-extractable generation tasks, and this limitation is not explicitly discussed (the Impact Statement is boilerplate and omits methodological limitations such as memory overhead, dependence on answer verifiers, and merging-related risks at larger ensemble sizes).

The paper is notation-heavy (three custom metrics, multiple reward variants, confidence calibration steps), which, combined with the volume of ablations spread across main text and appendix, makes the overall contribution somewhat dense to parse and could obscure which components matter most for practitioners.
